title: Polyperchon
capsule: Polyperchon was a Macedonian general who served Alexander the Great at Gaugamela (331 BCE) and rose to become regent of Macedon in 319 BCE when the dying Antipater passed over his own son Cassander and appointed Polyperchon in his stead. He attempted to stabilize the Argead succession by championing Philip III Arrhidaeus and then Alexander IV, issuing edicts restoring Greek city autonomy (318 BCE) to build a support coalition. Outmaneuvered by Cassander and Antigonus, he was stripped of effective power by 317 BCE and reduced to holding fragments of the Peloponnese; his final political act was ordering the execution of Heracles, Alexander's son by Barsine, in 309 BCE on Cassander's behalf. He survived into extreme old age — reportedly past ninety — as an irrelevant survivor of the Diadoch wars.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Polyperchon's role and chronology are well attested in Diodorus Siculus and Plutarch, but the territorial extent of his control at any given moment is poorly defined and changes rapidly; the attestation window 318–315 BCE reflects his regency and Peloponnesian phase rather than a stable territory.
